summary:
In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Samuel are a single book, divided in two by its ancient Greek translation; it is anonymous (Samuel, its namesake, dies before it ends) and set in the eleventh century BC, as the rule of the judges gives way to monarchy. Three lives carry the story: Samuel, the last judge; Saul, the first king; David, anointed to replace him. It opens with Hannah, childless and taunted by her husband's other wife, vowing at the sanctuary in Shiloh that if God gives her a son, she will give him back: "no razor shall ever touch his head" (1:11). Samuel is born, and Hannah's thanksgiving (2:1–10) previews the book's reversals — "The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble are equipped with strength" (2:4) — and ends on a king Israel does not yet have: "He will exalt the horn of His anointed" (2:10). Mary's song in Luke 1:46–55 echoes it closely. "Anointed" translates the Hebrew mashiach, the word that becomes "Messiah"; kings were set apart by oil poured on the head.

Samuel grows up under Eli the priest, whose sons steal from the sacrifices; in a day when "the word of the LORD was rare" (3:1), God calls the boy by name in the night. The Philistines, Israel's enemies on the coastal plain, capture the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the Law, and send it back after plagues strike their cities. When Samuel is old, the elders demand, "appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations" (8:5). Samuel warns what a king will take — sons, daughters, fields, a tenth of everything — but God grants the request, with a verdict: "it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king" (8:7). Deuteronomy 17:14–20 had already allowed for a king; readers debate whether the fault is kingship itself or the wish to be like the nations.

Saul, a tall Benjamite found searching for his father's donkeys, is anointed and made king. Two failures end him: he offers a sacrifice he was ordered to wait for — "the LORD has sought a man after His own heart" (13:14), Samuel tells him — and, sent to destroy the Amalekites, he spares their king and the best livestock; Samuel answers, "obedience is better than sacrifice" (15:22). In Bethlehem, God passes over seven sons of Jesse, and Samuel anoints the youngest, the shepherd David: "man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart" (16:7). David fells the Philistine champion Goliath — "six cubits and a span" in the standard Hebrew text, over nine feet, though some ancient copies read four cubits and a span, about six foot nine — and the women's victory song, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands" (18:7), makes Saul his enemy.

Saul's jealousy turns to hurled spears and manhunts; his son Jonathan, the heir apparent, sides with David in a covenant of friendship. The rest of the book is David the fugitive: caves, a band of the distressed and indebted, refuge among the Philistines. Twice he has Saul at his mercy and refuses to harm "the LORD's anointed" (24:6; 26:9–11). Samuel dies (25:1); before his final battle Saul, who had banned mediums, disguises himself and has a medium at Endor call Samuel up: "tomorrow you and your sons will be with me" (28:19). On Mount Gilboa the Philistines kill Jonathan and his brothers, and Saul falls on his own sword. The men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve his body from the wall of Beth-shan and bury the bones; 2 Samuel opens with David hearing the news.
